title: Do Deterministic Verifiers Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Paired Shared‑Candidate Evaluation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) to measure whether coupling a deterministic NetOps verifier+gate (generate→validate→repair, max 1 automated repair) to a single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) changes safety outcomes when the identical initial LLM candidate is observed with and without gating. Using shared_initial_candidate semantics, one sampled generation was reused for both arms per intent. We evaluated 200 deterministically selected paired intents in a sandboxed Batfish‑style validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All 200 shared initial candidates passed validation in both baseline and guarded arms (contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered paired estimand (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). No automated repairs were applied. We explain how shared_initial_candidate semantics, task‑bank alignment, and validator tightness produced this degenerate null, and we give artifact‑grounded recommendations for follow‑up preregistered designs that avoid ceiling effects.

sections.introduction: Generative language models are being investigated for intent→configuration translation and other NetOps tasks. Operational adoption requires evidence that model outputs will not introduce reachability, policy, or sequencing violations when applied to networks. Prior surveys and empirical reports emphasize that operational trustworthiness depends strongly on surrounding system machinery—retrieval, deterministic validators, gates, and repair loops—rather than the model alone [1]–[3]. Architectures that combine generation with external deterministic validation and bounded repair (generate→validate→repair) are widely advocated, but reproducible paired evidence that isolates the verifier/gate effect on identical model candidates is limited. We ask: for an intent→configuration task bank and a single LLM, does coupling a deterministic validator and deterministic accept/reject gate (with at most one automated repair) to the identical sampled initial candidate reduce the incidence of unsafe proposals relative to observing that same candidate without gating? We formalized this as the preregistered estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics and executed a fully preregistered confirmatory run (n=200 paired intents).
sections.related_work: Recent NetOps/AIOps literature documents both the promise and the safety risks of LLM‑assisted automation and repeatedly recommends augmenting generative models with external verification and constrained repair [1]–[3]. Benchmarks for log analysis and retrieval‑quality emphasize pipeline-level evaluation but often lack tightly coupled intent→config items with deterministic validators [4]. In adjacent domains, generate–validate–repair pipelines have improved outcomes under specific datasets and validators: autonomous program‑repair agents show measurable repair gains under controlled benchmarks [5], and LLM agents applied to infrastructure code and DevOps tasks report reductions in manifested errors when verifier or test‑based checks are used as a gate [6],[7]. These domain findings motivate testing verifier/gate value in NetOps but do not guarantee the same effect under different task banks, model prompts, or validator rule sets.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design. We preregistered study autocand_A1_prereg_v1 and froze the primary estimand, generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate), model, deterministic validator, gate policy, repair budget (≤1 automatic repair), task selection rule (deterministic adapter index), and analysis executor before observing any outputs. The confirmatory design is paired: for each intent a single LLM generation is produced and deterministically reused by both the baseline (observe) and guarded (validate+gate+optional single repair) conditions; under shared_initial_candidate semantics only validator/repair/gate can change outcomes. Model and validator. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementing Batfish‑style sequencing, precondition, final_group and minimum_up rules, and reachability/policy checks. Implementation notes and archival practice. Model configuration recorded max_output_tokens=2000 and maximum_attempts_per_call=1. The model configuration file records temperature=null; null/unset temperature does not imply deterministic sampling (temperature=0) and the adapter does not guarantee deterministic model sampling. The runtime semantics used one sampled initial generation per pair which the adapter reused for both arms; this single shared draw is central to the estimand's interpretation. Primary outcome and analysis. The binary primary outcome unsafe_flag is true if the validator reports any reachability or workflow/policy violation after candidate stabilization. The preregistered confirmatory analysis used a paired‑binary executor (exact McNemar‑equivalent) and a paired‑bootstrap percentile CI (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000). Missing‑data and retry policies were fixed in preregistration; no retriable infrastructure failures occurred.
sections.results: Execution accounting. The run executed as preregistered and completed without failures. One shared initial model call was produced per pair (200 model calls total), and all pairs produced archived shared candidates that were fed to both arms. Primary outcome. The paired 2×2 contingency is n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0: every shared initial candidate was scored VALID_CONFIGURATION by the deterministic validator in both baseline and guarded arms. The paired estimate (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000). Repair activity. No automated repairs were applied in any guarded episode (repair_applied=false for all pairs). Diagnostics and representative episodes. Representative tasks exercise sequencing constraints (VLAN migrations, uplink failover, MTU upgrades), protected interfaces, and final_group/minimum_up policies. Validator diagnostics for examples show parsed_command_count matching required_command_count and violation_count=0, consistent with syntactically correct mappings from the model's outputs to the required sequences.
sections.discussion: Artifact‑grounded interpretation. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory estimand isolates only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates. Observing n11=200 implies that, for the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), the synthetic task bank, the prompt/template family, and the validator rule set, the sampled initial candidates already satisfied the validator constraints; therefore the guarded pipeline applied no repairs and changed no acceptance decisions. The zero‑width bootstrap CI and p=1.0 are a direct consequence of complete concordance and represent a valid inferential outcome under the preregistered estimand. Contributors to this ceiling effect supported by archived artifacts include: (1) task‑bank alignment—a deterministic task generator produced required_sequence forms closely matching the prompt schema, increasing the probability of model outputs that syntactically satisfy constraints; (2) validator tightness—the validator encoded the same sequencing and precondition checks used in task synthesis so correct syntactic mappings pass validation readily; and (3) shared_initial_candidate semantics prevented any guarded‑conditioned regeneration or model sampling variance that might have yielded discordant outcomes. Design implications and recommendations. To obtain nondegenerate evidence of verifier/gate utility we recommend preregistered follow‑ups that intentionally increase baseline unsafe rates or permit model variance to manifest: (a) adversarial or out‑of‑distribution task injection to raise baseline error rates; (b) an independent‑generation per‑condition confirmatory design (two independent model draws per paired intent) so the estimand captures guarded‑conditioned regeneration and sampling variance (this requires up to two model calls per pair and an updated power calculation); (c) evaluating multiple model variants or sampling temperatures to expose sampling sensitivity; (d) expanding automated repair budgets or iterative repair loops to evaluate repair efficacy when initial violations are nontrivial; and (e) adding human‑in‑the‑loop arms to measure operator decision behavior in response to validator flags. Operational caveats. This null result is specific to the experimental frame (single model, synthetic tasks, deterministic validator, shared_initial_candidate semantics) and does not imply deterministic validators lack value in production or adversarial regimes.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics comparing an LLM‑alone observation to the same initial candidate after deterministic verification and bounded automated repair. Every sampled initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator and the guarded pipeline applied no repairs; the paired difference = 0.0 (p = 1.0) with a paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]. This null outcome is an artifact of the preregistered generation semantics, task synthesis alignment, and validator rule coverage. We archive full artifacts and recommend follow‑up preregistered designs (independent per‑condition generation, adversarial tasks, multiple model draws, and expanded repair budgets) that deliberately avoid ceiling effects and can quantify verifier/gate contributions under more challenging conditions.

limitations: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean baseline and guarded conditions began from an identical initial candidate; the confirmatory estimand therefore measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that candidate and cannot assess effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or multiple independent model samples.

Construct validity: tasks were synthetic and deterministically selected; the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (sequencing, reachability, and workflow rules) and may not capture other operational risks (transient performance regressions, vendor‑specific side effects outside validator rules).

External validity: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, and synthetic intents limit generalizability to other models, validators, production topologies, or live device interactions.

Conclusion validity: the observed null effect (paired difference = 0) reflects this execution's sampling frame where baseline generation produced only valid candidates; the study was powered to detect ~10 percentage‑point reductions but cannot rule out smaller effects under different sampling or adversarial inputs.
Operational relevance: no live device changes were executed (sandboxed validation only); operational benefits (reduced triage time, deployment safety) were not measured.
Security/contamination: adversarial or poisoning scenarios were not exercised; no retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) was used, so retrieval‑based poisoning vectors were not evaluated.

Task‑bank reporting: the archived task manifest contains per‑task difficulty labels; manifest metadata indicates the bank is dominated by 'very_hard' items with a minority labeled 'extreme' (exact per‑label counts are available in the archived manifest).
